doc.title: Nick Brignola interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 28, 1997

title: Three and a half months with Woody Herman
summary: He corrects the 'year' with Woody, mentions Mike Brignola, Sal Nistico helping him solo, and leaving in 1963-64 amid road weariness and family troubles.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: I didn’t ask you about — you had a year with Woody Herman?

No, hell no. How about like three and a half months or something like that. There’s two Brignolas. There’s Mike Brignola, who is with Woody Herman’s band now, happens to be the baritone player too. He has the record for being probably next to Frank Tiberi, the guy the most, the fellow that’s been with Woody Herman’s band the longest. He joined in 1979 and has been the baritone player since then. Coincidentally, we have the same name, and we play the same instrument. He’s about twenty years younger than I am. His name is Mike. And we think we might be related because his ancestry kind of is from the same area of Italy as mine. Anyway, to make a long story short, I wasn’t with Woody’s band too — I told you before, I didn’t like big bands, I didn’t feel comfortable in big bands. And most big bands didn’t feature the baritone player too much, you know the tenor, especially Woody’s band, was mostly tenor. But I got to play a lot actually, due to the efforts of Sal Nistico, who got me on the band. Sal used to say to Woody, you know, “Let him play.” And Woody would say, “Well we don’t have any chart for him.” “Well let him play on one of my tunes,” you know, Sal was gracious in that respect. And I got to play, you know. And as I remember when I did leave the band, Woody said to me, “Man, we’re just starting to write some charts for you, why are you leaving?” But it was at a time in my life when I just had to get out, I just couldn’t’ do it.

Yeah, most of it was, but it was also like there’s an album called “Woody Herman 1964” on the Phillips label. If you look on the back there, it was recorded the day Kennedy got killed, November 22, we were in the studio recording that day. And I had just — my second daughter was born, and I was kind of —you know, the President gets killed, my daughter was born with a liver problem, I’m on the road, I didn’t really like it, so I just said who needs it, so I left. And those other two incidents helped me make my decision. But it was a musical decision too. But what was funny is Woody asked me to come back, I mean throughout the years Woody would say, “Any time you want to come back” you know. And one time they were going to Japan and I was tempted because I had never been to Japan and I was going to go. And then something happened where I was going to do something with my own group, that fusion group I had. And I just felt well gee, you know, realistically I’ve got to do my own thing and let’s go with this. And in retrospect I should have gone with Woody. But it would have been nice. But I always saw Woody, right up until he died, you know the year he died I saw him all the time, we hung out and laughed and reminisced and whatever.
